title: Translations carry no governance weight and always lose to the English original on any discrepancy
content:
A.1.2.2.2.23 defines Translation Documents, addressed by suffixing the original's identifier with a language code (a Spanish translation of A.1 becomes A.1.es). They mirror the original's components with names and data translated. They should be updated whenever the original is, "however, in case of any discrepancies or contradictions, the original English version of the Atlas Document always takes precedence."

The Type Overview is blunt about the trade: translations "do not have any impact on the governance or operation of Sky, but they are important for accessibility and inclusivity."

This is a deliberate refusal of a hard problem. A framework built on spirit-of-the-rule interpretation and precise term annotation cannot survive N co-equal language versions — every translation choice would become a potential Atlas Interpretation, and contradictions between languages would multiply the defect surface the Core Facilitator must repair. Nominating one canonical language collapses that entirely.

The honest cost is that non-English participants read a document that is explicitly not the rule. Combined with the Element Annotation machinery — where governance turns on the bounded meaning of specific English words — this means full participation in interpretation is effectively English-gated, whatever the accessibility intent. The Atlas accepts that rather than pretending translations are equivalent, which is at least the more auditable failure mode.

It is also consistent with the identifier scheme: Accessory Documents are marked by containing letters, so a translation's non-authoritative status is visible in its address.
description: A.1.2.2.2.23 classifies Translation Documents as Accessory with 'no impact on the governance or operation of Sky', resolving multilingual ambiguity by fiat rather than by interpretation.
